5.1.2.2: Closed functionality must be usable without the user attaching, connecting, or installing assistive technology, and must meet clauses 5.1.3 to 5.1.6 as applicable. Personal headsets and personal induction loops do not count as assistive technology here.
5.1.3.1: Where visual information is needed to use closed functionality, the ICT must provide at least one non-visual way to use it that includes auditory output.
5.1.3.6: Where closed functionality presents non-text content other than video, any alternative for it must be delivered as auditory output including speech, unless the content is pure decoration or visual formatting only.
5.1.3.7: Where pre-recorded video is needed to use closed functionality, the ICT must provide an auditory equivalent for that video, and must pass on any auditory equivalent supplied with video from another source.
5.1.6.1: Where closed functionality cannot be operated with a keyboard or keyboard interface, it must still be operable without vision as clause 5.1.3 requires.
5.5: ICT that needs manual operation must offer a mode in which every manually operated function can be controlled without vision, using only parts that can be found and told apart by touch (a screen edge, corner, or tactile marker counts).
6.0.2: A communication client that supports real-time voice with or within a communication system must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 and 6.3 to 6.6 when communicating, and, if it is part of a terminal that handles text, every applicable clause 6.2 (RTT) requirement too.
6.0.3: A communication system that provides real-time voice to its own clients must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 to 6.6 when communicating with them. Component parts such as routers can be tested by including them in a system under test.
6.0.4: A communication system that connects to other real-time voice systems must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 to 6.6 when communicating with those other systems.
6.0.5: A communication system that accepts a visiting (roaming) client from another compatible system must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 to 6.6 when communicating with that visiting client.
6.0.6: A communication client that provides emergency communications must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 and 6.3 to 6.6 during an emergency communication, plus all applicable clause 6.2 (RTT) requirements where the terminal handles text.
6.0.7: A communication system that carries real-time voice emergency communications to public safety answering points (PSAPs) must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 to 6.6 during the emergency communication.
6.0.8: A communication system handling an emergency communication from a visiting (roaming) client of another system must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 to 6.6 when connecting that client to a PSAP.
6.0.9: A communication system whose own client is in another country must meet every applicable requirement of clauses 6.1 to 6.6 when that client contacts a PSAP in the visited country. This covers VoIP-style systems that do not use call-control roaming.
6.1.1: ICT that connects to other ICT for real-time voice must document the specifications it uses so that voice interoperates, covering at least 100 Hz to 7 000 Hz, either by mutual agreement with the other ICT or by implementing ITU-T G.722.
6.1.2: ICT with a user interface for real-time voice must be able to capture, communicate, and present speech over a frequency range of at least 250 Hz to 7 000 Hz.
6.1.3: Advisory: ICT with an interface for external presentation of voice (such as attached listening devices) should be able to present audio from at least 100 Hz up to 7 000 Hz.
6.1.4: Advisory: where subtitles are provided for real-time voice communication, the delay between a word being spoken and its first character appearing should not exceed 2 seconds.
6.2.1.1: ICT that provides real-time voice communication must also provide real-time text (RTT) communication, which implicitly covers interoperation for RTT wherever it interoperates for voice, and multi-party RTT where multi-party voice is supported.
6.2.1.2: Where ICT provides real-time voice and supports RTT, it must allow voice and RTT to be used at the same time.
6.2.1.3: ICT with RTT must let a single user action act on all requested or established media (voice, RTT, and any other media) when starting, answering, modifying, holding, transferring, or ending a communication.
6.2.2.1: Displayed RTT must show text from different sources, and the text the user sends, with each source indicated and told apart; a simple identifier such as Speaker 1 is enough.
6.2.2.2: Where ICT provides speaker indication for voice, it must indicate every active communicator, including those using RTT, so all parties know who is communicating.
6.2.2.3: ICT that supports RTT must display a real-time indicator of non-local audio activity, so a user who cannot hear knows when someone is speaking.
6.2.2.4: RTT must be presented as blocks of text from each source, including the local user, ordered by the moment each block ends (sentence-ending punctuation plus a space, a line separator, or a 5-second pause); editing a block moves it to the time of the last edit.
6.2.2.5: Users must be able to review the whole RTT content of a communication while it is in progress and, if the communication is recorded, after it has ended.
6.2.3: A communication client that supports touch-tone (DTMF) signalling on voice calls must provide a way to send touch-tones for the characters 0 to 9, star, hash, and A to D that is distinct from typing those characters as RTT and compatible with the standard method for voice calls.
6.2.5: The RTT user interface must let users enter new text and erase text from the current end of what they typed, without being blocked by a new line or other delimiter in earlier text; automatic corrections count as erasure too.
6.2.6: ICT that supports multi-party communication with RTT must be able to receive and process RTT at a total of 90 characters per second from at least 3 simultaneous sources sending 30 characters per second each.
6.2.7: RTT must handle at least a subset of ISO/IEC 10646 that covers Latin-1, the writing directions and characters of the languages of the intended regions, any emoji the platform supports, the replacement character U+FFFD for lost or unsupported characters, and any characters the presentation protocol uses.
6.2.8: A communication client that supports RTT must accept RTT input through every method the ICT offers for general text input.
6.2.9: Regardless of system or client settings, it must be possible to request a communication with RTT media, to answer a request and have RTT added whether or not it was in the original request, and for any party to upgrade an existing communication to include RTT.
6.2.10: ICT that connects to other ICT for real-time voice must document how its RTT interoperates with that other ICT, either by mutual agreement or, as the fallback, by implementing ITU-T T.140 with IETF RFC 4103 as updated by RFC 9071.
6.5.5: Where real-time video is part of voice communication, the ICT must provide a real-time indicator of audio activity, so a user who cannot hear knows when someone is talking.
6.5.6: Where ICT provides speaker indication for voice users in video communication, it must indicate every active communicator, including those who are signing.
6.7.1: ICT that provides real-time voice and includes real-time video must provide total conversation: RTT meeting clause 6.2, voice meeting clause 6.1, and video meeting clause 6.5, while also meeting clauses 6.3 and 6.4.
6.7.2: ICT that connects to other ICT for voice and video must document the specifications by which its video interoperates with that other ICT, either by mutual agreement or by implementing ITU-T H.264 (at least version 10, constrained baseline level 3) and, where codecs are negotiated, H.265 or VP8 to avoid transcoding.
7.1.1: ICT that displays video with synchronized audio must have a mode that displays the available subtitles, and where closed subtitles are part of the content, must let the user choose to display them.
7.1.2: Where ICT displays subtitles, each subtitle must appear within 100 ms of the timecode attached to it.
7.1.3: ICT that transmits, converts, or records video with synchronized audio must preserve subtitle data, including presentational data such as screen position, colours, text style, and fonts, so the subtitles can still be displayed as clause 7.1.1 requires.
7.1.4: Where ICT controls how its subtitles are presented, users must be able to adapt the displayed characteristics of subtitles to their own needs, except where subtitles are displayed as unmodifiable characters.
7.3: ICT whose primary purpose is playing video with synchronized audio, and which controls the activation of subtitles, audio description, and spoken subtitles, must let the user switch any of those on or off with a single action at the same level of interaction as the volume control.
8.2.1.1: Hardware with speech output that is typically held to the ear must let the user raise the speech volume to at least 18 dB of conversational gain.
8.2.2.1: Fixed-line communication devices and wired handsets held to the ear must provide magnetic coupling to hearing technologies meeting ETSI ES 200 381-1, and must be marked as compatible with magnetic coupling if designed for public use.
8.3.2: Display screens that are part of stationary ICT must be placed so that no part of the display is lower than 800 mm above the floor of the access space.
8.3.3.1: Where nothing in the design prevents it, all information needed to operate stationary ICT must be placed no higher than 1 600 mm above the floor of the access space (Set 1).
8.3.3.2: Where functional or design requirements prevent placing it lower, information needed to operate stationary ICT must be placed no higher than 2 000 mm above the floor of the access space (Set 2).
8.3.5.1: Where operable parts can be placed or duplicated freely, at least one of each type must sit between 800 mm and 1 100 mm above the floor (Set 1).
8.3.5.2: Where operable parts cannot be duplicated or placed in the 800 mm to 1 100 mm band, those parts must sit between 380 mm and 1 220 mm above the floor and must not be blocked by obstructions (Set 2).
8.3.6: At least one of each type of operable part on stationary ICT must lie within a horizontal span of no more than 900 mm, so users do not have to move to reach all controls.
8.3.7.1: Where operable parts can be placed or duplicated freely, at least one of each type must be within 300 mm of the edge of the ICT nearest the user (Set 1).
8.3.7.2: Where operable parts cannot be duplicated or placed within 300 mm, at least one of each type must be within 510 mm (forward reach) or 610 mm (side reach) of the edge of the ICT nearest the user (Set 2).
8.3.9.2: Where stationary ICT has an integral obstruction in front of the controls and nothing requires it to be deeper than 300 mm, the obstruction must be no higher than 800 mm and no deeper than 300 mm (Set 1).
8.3.9.3: Where functional or design constraints require a deeper front obstruction, it must be no higher than 800 mm and no deeper than 510 mm (Set 2).
8.3.10.2: Where stationary ICT has an integral obstruction to the side of the controls and nothing requires it to be deeper than 300 mm, the obstruction must be no higher than 800 mm and no deeper than 300 mm (Set 1).
8.3.10.3: Where functional or design constraints require a deeper side obstruction, it must be no higher than 865 mm and no deeper than 610 mm (Set 2).
8.3.11.1: Where nothing prevents it, stationary ICT must provide knee and toe clearance underneath with the Set 1 dimensions of Table 8.2: a clear width of 900 mm (or the width of the ICT), at least 700 mm of height under an obstruction, and the table's minimum knee and toe depths.
8.3.11.2: Where design requirements restrict the open space below stationary ICT, it must still provide knee and toe clearance with the Set 2 dimensions of Table 8.2: a clear width of 760 mm (or the width of the ICT), at least 685 mm of height under an obstruction, and the table's reduced knee and toe depths.
8.4.2.1: Hardware with operable parts that need grasping, pinching, or twisting of the wrist must offer at least one way to operate them that does not require those actions.
8.4.2.2: Hardware controls that need more than 22.2 N of force must have an alternative means of operation that needs 22.2 N or less.
8.4.3: Keys, tickets, and cards whose orientation matters for further use must have an orientation that can be discerned by touch.
8.7: Where colour on hardware conveys information, it must not be the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.
8.8: Printed characters and symbols needed for use, and unlabelled operable parts that cannot be discerned by touch, must contrast visually with their background as light on dark or dark on light; a Michelson contrast of 0.7 for characters and 0.4 for controls is the usual approach.
9.1.2.2: Captions (called subtitles in EN 301 549) are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media.
9.1.2.4: Captions (called subtitles in EN 301 549) are provided for all live audio content in synchronized media.
9.2.4.11: When a component receives keyboard focus, it is not entirely hidden by author-created content.
9.2.5.7: Functionality that uses dragging has a single pointer alternative, unless dragging is essential.
9.2.5.8: Target size is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels except in specific cases (spacing, equivalent control, inline, user-agent control, essential).
9.3.2.6: Help mechanisms appear in the same relative order across pages within a set of web pages.
9.3.3.7: Information previously entered in a process is either auto-populated or selectable, unless re-entering it is essential or for security.
9.3.3.8: Authentication methods do not rely solely on cognitive function tests such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle.
9.7: A web page must not block the browser's modes of operation that present it according to user preference settings, and must not explicitly override user preferences for documented platform accessibility features (colour filters, contrast, text size, pointer size, text cursor) unless that is essential to the page.
10.1.2.2: Captions (called subtitles in EN 301 549) are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media.
10.1.2.4: Captions (called subtitles in EN 301 549) are provided for all live audio content in synchronized media.
10.2.4.2: Where the document format has a programmatically determinable title that common authoring tools can edit, the document has a title that describes its name, topic, or purpose.
10.2.4.11: Where the document accepts keyboard input, a component that receives keyboard focus is not entirely hidden by author-created content.
10.2.5.7: Functionality that uses dragging has a single pointer alternative, unless dragging is essential or determined by the user agent rather than the author.
10.2.5.8: Target size is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels except in specific cases (spacing, equivalent control, inline, user-agent control, essential).
10.3.1.1: The default human language of each non-web document can be programmatically determined.
10.3.2.3: Within a set of non-web documents, navigational mechanisms that repeat across documents occur in the same relative order each time, unless the user changes it.
10.3.2.4: Within a set of non-web documents, components with the same functionality are identified consistently.
10.3.2.6: Within a set of non-web documents, repeated help mechanisms (human contact details, contact mechanism, self-help, automated contact) appear in the same relative order, unless the user changes it.
10.3.3.7: Information previously entered in a process is either auto-populated or selectable, unless re-entering it is essential or for security.
10.3.3.8: Authentication steps in a document do not rely solely on cognitive function tests unless an alternative, assistance, object recognition, or personal content is offered.
10.5: Advisory: subtitles in synchronized media inside a non-web document should not obscure relevant information in the media.
10.7: A non-web document must not block the user agent's modes of operation that present it according to user preference settings, and must not explicitly override user preferences for documented platform accessibility features unless that is essential to the document.
11.1.2.2: Captions (called subtitles in EN 301 549) are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media.
11.1.2.4: Captions (called subtitles in EN 301 549) are provided for all live audio content in synchronized media.
11.2.4.2: Where the platform supports title attributes for windows or screens, each window or screen has a title that describes its name, topic, or purpose.
11.2.4.11: Where the software accepts keyboard input, a component that receives keyboard focus is not entirely hidden by author-created content.
11.2.5.7: Functionality that uses dragging has a single pointer alternative, unless dragging is essential or determined by the platform rather than the author.
11.2.5.8: Target size is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels except in specific cases (spacing, equivalent control, inline, platform control, essential).
11.3.1.1: The default human language of the software's open functionality can be programmatically determined.
11.3.2.4: Components with the same functionality within the software are identified consistently, unless not doing so is essential.
11.3.3.7: Information previously entered in a process is either auto-populated or selectable, unless re-entering it is essential or for security.
11.3.3.8: Authentication steps in the software do not rely solely on cognitive function tests unless an alternative, assistance, object recognition, or personal content is offered.
11.5.2.1: Platform software must provide a documented set of platform accessibility services covering every user interface concept of clauses 11.5.2.5 to 11.5.2.17 that the platform supports, either its own or those of its underlying platform.
12.1: Information about a product that is made available digitally must itself conform to clause 9 (web), clause 10 (non-web document), or clause 11 (non-web software), depending on the format it is delivered in.
12.2: Information about a service, including support services, that is made available digitally must itself conform to clause 9 (web), clause 10 (non-web document), or clause 11 (non-web software), depending on the format it is delivered in.
12.4: An electronic programme guide must provide information on whether subtitles, audio description, spoken subtitles, and sign language interpretation are available for the media it lists.
12.5: Where an electronic programme guide has information about the accessibility features of a media item, it must offer a mode in which users can find out whether subtitles, audio description, spoken subtitles, or sign language are available without activating the item.
13.1.2.2: Relay service invocation functions must use the destination addresses that primary users receive from their own communication systems, so the relay service does not require special numbers.
13.1.2.3: The caller identifier of a primary user of a relay service must be conveyed to the secondary user when the communication is established, unless the calling equipment is set to anonymous mode.
13.1.2.4: Primary users must be able to decide, by their own action at the moment they start an outgoing communication, whether a relay service is invoked.
13.1.2.5: Primary users must be able to decide, by their own action at the moment they receive an incoming communication, whether a relay service is invoked.
13.1.2.6: On the primary user's request, the ICT must initiate and carry out an emergency communication and invoke the relay service in it.
13.1.3.1: A relay service must let primary users take part in speech communication with secondary users by converting modality (text, sign language, lip-speaking, clear speech) or providing communication support according to the type of relay service.
13.1.3.2: Relay service invocation functions must pass through any media that are not being converted but are enabled by the primary and secondary users' communication clients.
13.1.3.3: A relay service must support the participation of primary users in conferences, with the extra modality conversion conveyed via the conference system or directly between the relay service and its user.
13.1.3.4: A relay service must accept invocations from emergency communication PSAPs, in a three-party fashion as specified in ETSI EN 303 919.
4.2.1: Where ICT has visual modes of operation, it must provide at least one mode of operation that does not require vision. Annex C treats each criterion in clause 4.2 as met when the Annex B requirements mapped to it are met, or when there is evidence of the outcome.
4.2.2: Where ICT has visual modes of operation, it must provide features, such as magnification, a reduced field of vision, or control of contrast, brightness and intensity, that let people with limited vision use it.
4.2.3: Where ICT has visual modes of operation, it must provide a visual mode that does not depend on the user perceiving colour.
4.2.4: Where ICT has auditory modes of operation, it must provide at least one mode of operation that does not require hearing.
4.2.5: Where ICT has auditory modes of operation, it must provide enhanced audio features, such as clarity enhancement, background-noise reduction, a wider volume range, or a way to connect assistive listening devices.
4.2.6: Where ICT requires vocal input, it must provide at least one mode of operation that does not require the user to produce speech or other vocal sounds.
4.2.7: Where ICT requires manual actions, it must provide features that let users operate it through alternative actions that do not need fine manipulation, simultaneous actions, or hand strength.
4.2.8: Where ICT is stationary, free-standing, or installed, every element needed to operate it must be within reach of all users, including wheelchair users and people of different statures.
4.2.9: Where ICT has visual modes of operation, its default mode must minimise the potential for triggering photosensitive seizures, or, for audiovisual material, warn in advance that triggers may be present.
4.2.10: Where ICT provides information or requires interaction, it must provide features or presentation that make it simpler and easier to understand, operate, and use, such as adjustable timings, error suggestions, a logical focus order, audio output of text, and tasks broken into easy steps.
4.2.11: Where ICT provides accessibility features, using them must not reduce the user's privacy: for example private listening through a personal headset, no spoken version of masked characters, and user control over legal, financial, and personal data.
5.1.3.3: Where closed functionality provides auditory output and information is displayed on screen, the auditory output must let the user correlate what they hear with what is on the display.
5.10.1: Authoring tools must meet clauses 5.10.2 to 5.10.5 to the extent that the output format supports the relevant accessibility information.
5.10.2: Authoring tools must enable and guide the production of content that conforms to clause 9 (web), clause 10 (non-web documents), or clause 11 (non-web software), as applicable.
5.10.4: Where an authoring tool can detect that content fails a requirement of clause 9, 10, or 11, it must offer repair suggestions.
7.1.5: ICT that displays video with synchronized audio must have a mode that plays spoken subtitles when they are available; it does not have to generate them from text subtitles.
9.6: Web pages must satisfy all five WCAG 2.2 conformance requirements at Level AA: conformance level, full pages, complete processes, only accessibility-supported ways of using technologies, and non-interference.
11.5.2.3: Advisory: software with open functionality should use the platform's documented accessibility services listed in 11.5.2.1, and other documented platform services where those do not suffice to meet 11.5.2.5 to 11.5.2.17.
11.7: Software that is not isolated from its platform must follow the user's platform accessibility preference settings, such as colour filters, contrast, text size, pointer size, and text cursor, unless not following a setting is essential to the software's function.
5.1.8: Where closed functionality has input fields that collect information about the user and serve one of the purposes listed in WCAG 2.2 (name, address, email and so on), at least one mode of operation must present the purpose of each field in audio.
